title: Companies may be selective, but pvt capex picking up: FM
syllabus: GS3 › Indian economy: growth, development and employment; Industrial policy (MSMEs, PLI); Investment · GS2 › Government policies and interventions; Governance · GS4 › Trust and public service values in governance
summary: The Finance Minister said private investment is picking up selectively after the GST 2.0 reforms, MSMEs are being helped to grow through a new definition, and the PLI scheme's weaker sectors will be examined, with trust in citizens as the government's charter.
evolution: Jan Vishwas and trust-based reforms: the challenge is wages, not jobs.
Editorial: the challenge is more productive employment.
FM: MSMEs must grow from micro to large; policy built on trusting people.
ideas: Demand-led investment revival: the FM said GST 2.0 reforms made consumption and demand visible, so industry is investing again, though selectively in chosen sectors.
GS3 · Investment / Growth
Private capex follows visible demand: consumption recovery is the trigger for a sustained investment cycle.
Micro should not remain dwarfs: the revised MSME definition lets micro firms grow into small, small into medium and medium into large while keeping benefits.
GS3 · MSMEs / Industrial policy
Removing the penalty on growth helps India fill its 'missing middle' of mid-sized firms.
Beyond a few big firms: the FM rejected the view that a few large groups dominate the economy, citing flourishing MSMEs and fast-growing startups and unicorns.
GS3 · Industry structure
A broad base of MSMEs and startups, not a few conglomerates, makes growth inclusive and resilient.
Incentives tied to performance: PLI pays only for additional production; it has worked, but sectors that underperformed will be examined.
GS3 · Industrial policy (PLI)
Linking incentives to output, and reviewing failures, keeps industrial policy accountable.
Trust as the charter of governance: GST, income tax and other policies are framed on trusting businesses, farmers, taxpayers and citizens, with active, continuous dialogue with industry.
GS2 · Governance / GS4 · Trust
A trust-based state treats citizens as partners, cutting compliance burden and building cooperation.
keywords: Too few mid-sized firms between many tiny ones and a few large ones
India's missing middle keeps productivity low; helping MSMEs scale up is the cure.
Loss of benefits that deters a firm from growing beyond a size limit
A revised MSME definition removes the graduation penalty that kept firms small.
Clarity about future demand that gives firms confidence to invest
Visible consumption demand, not tax breaks alone, revives private capex.
Policy that presumes citizens are honest and reduces control
Trust-based governance shifts the state from suspicion to facilitation.
Support paid only on measurable output
Performance-linked incentives make public money pay only for results.
data: Share of India's exports from the MSME sector
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, via IE
GS3 · MSMEs / Exports
MSMEs account for about 40% of India's exports (Finance Minister), so their growth is export growth.
examples: Revised MSME definition
Lets enterprises grow while keeping benefits
GS3 · Industrial policy · MSMEs
The revised MSME definition shows how policy can reward growth instead of penalising it.
PLI's performance condition
Incentive only for additional production
GS3 · Industrial policy · GS2 · Accountability
PLI paying only for extra output is an example of outcome-based public spending.
'We trust the taxpayer'
FM on trust as the basis of GST and income tax policy
GS4
GS2 · Governance · GS4 · Trust and public service values
The FM's stated charter of trusting taxpayers is an example of trust-based, citizen-centric governance.
pyqs: Manufacturing share and MSMEs for faster growth; present policies.
Rationale, achievements and improvement of the PLI scheme.
Industrial growth lagging GDP and recent industrial policy changes.
Labour-led growth and a growth pattern that creates more jobs.

trend.t: Industrial questions moved from why manufacturing lagged (2017) to MSMEs and manufacturing share in GDP (2023), then to evaluating specific tools such as PLI (2025) amid protectionism. The direction is clear: from describing the problem to judging policy instruments.
trend.watch: UPSC now asks you to evaluate schemes: rationale, achievements, improvements. Know PLI, the MSME definition, credit schemes and their limits.
focus: MSMEs: scaling up and the missing middle

potential: Why do most Indian MSMEs remain small? Discuss the 'missing middle' problem and suggest measures to help them scale up. (15 marks)
"Private investment follows demand, not incentives." Examine in the context of India's recent capex cycle. (10 marks)
What is trust-based governance? How does it change the relationship between the state and citizens? (10 marks)

practice.q: Why do most Indian MSMEs remain small? Discuss the 'missing middle' problem and suggest measures to help them scale up.
parts: Measures to help them scale up

answer.t: MSMEs produce about 40% of India's exports (Finance Minister, Nov 2026), yet most stay micro; the government says it wants micro firms to grow into small, medium and large ones.

pts.t: Firms lose subsidies, reservations and tax benefits once they cross size limits, so they stay small.
pts.ex: The revised definition aims to remove this.

pts.t: Lack of collateral and formal records limits access to bank loans.
Large buyers and governments pay late, choking working capital.
Many inspections, filings and licences cost more for small firms.
pts.ex: Jan Vishwas decriminalisation is a response.

pts.t: Old machines and untrained workers keep productivity low.
Many firms stay outside the formal system to avoid tax and regulation.
Tiny firms cannot reach economies of scale.
Most employment is informal and low-paid.
pts.ex: Link: 'the challenge is wages, not jobs' (IE, 2 Nov).

pts.t: Few firms are large enough to supply global value chains.
A few large groups dominate while the base stays weak.

answer.h: Measures to help them scale up

pts.t: Let firms keep benefits for a period after crossing thresholds.
Lend on digital transaction records, not just collateral.
pts.ex: TReDS for invoice discounting; CGTMSE credit guarantees.

pts.t: Penalise late payments to MSMEs.
Self-certification, fewer inspections, decriminalised minor offences.
pts.ex: FM: policy built on trusting business.

pts.t: Common facilities, testing labs and tool rooms for MSME clusters.

pts.k: Link to big firms and PLI
pts.t: Bring MSMEs into supply chains of large manufacturers and incentive schemes.
Apprenticeships and easy registration bring firms into the formal economy.

answer.t: India will become a manufacturing power only when its micro firms are free and able to grow; trust, credit and a growth-friendly policy can fill the missing middle.

title: The challenge is more productive employment
syllabus: GS3 › Inclusive growth; Employment; Growth and development · GS1 › Poverty; Role of women; Migration · GS2 › Issues relating to poverty
summary: With extreme poverty down to 2.6%, the editorial argues the next obstacle to mass prosperity is the lack of productive, better-paid non-farm jobs.
evolution: World Bank: extreme poverty falls to 2.6% in 2023; poverty concentrated in the UP–West Bengal belt (front page).
Manish Sabharwal: 'Challenge is wages, not jobs' (editorial page).
Editorial: the challenge is more productive employment.
ideas: Poverty fell, productivity did not follow: extreme poverty is down to 2.6% and the $4.2 line to 16.1%, but the lack of productive, better-paid non-farm jobs now blocks mass prosperity.
GS3 · Inclusive growth
India's next development challenge is not poverty reduction alone but productive employment.
More workers, not better work: labour force participation has risen, mostly as women join, but many are in farming or self-employment.
GS3 · Employment / GS1 · Women
Rising participation driven by women in farm and self-employment adds workers without raising productivity.
Stalled structural transformation: agriculture still employs a large share of workers compared with China and Vietnam, and most non-farm workers are in informal, low-productivity firms.
GS3 · Structural transformation
India's workforce has not moved out of farming at the pace East Asian economies managed.
Manufacturing missed its role: unlike other Asian economies, Indian manufacturing has not absorbed low-skilled workers; jobs grew in low-end services instead.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Without labour-intensive manufacturing, workers leaving farms crowd into low-end services.
Geography of jobs: poverty is concentrated in the UP–West Bengal belt, where incomes and jobs are scarce, so migration to richer regions is the main route to non-farm work.
GS1 · Migration / Regional disparity
Regional job deserts make migration the default escape route from poverty.
keywords: Shift of workers from low- to high-productivity sectors
Moving up the income ladder requires structural transformation of the workforce.
Manufacturing peaking early, before absorbing surplus labour
India shows signs of premature deindustrialisation, with services absorbing low-skilled labour.
Growth stalling before reaching high income
Low-productivity jobs risk trapping India below upper-middle income.
Moving for work because local options are absent
Job scarcity in the eastern belt drives distress migration.
Industries employing many low-skilled workers per unit of capital
Labour-intensive manufacturing is the missing bridge from farm to formal work.

World Bank, via IE
GS1 · Poverty
Extreme poverty fell to 2.6% in 2023, and the $4.2-line rate fell from 57.7% to 16.1% (World Bank).

World Bank, via IE

examples: China and Vietnam's farm-to-factory shift
Smaller farm workforces after manufacturing absorbed labour
GS3 · Structural transformation · GS1 · Globalisation
China and Vietnam show how labour-intensive manufacturing moves workers out of farming.
UP–West Bengal poverty belt

GS1 · Migration, regional disparity · GS3 · Inclusive growth
The UP–West Bengal belt shows why place-based job creation is central to ending poverty.
pyqs: Labour-led growth and job creation without hurting productivity.
Why manufacturing failed at labour-intensive exports.

trend.t: Employment questions moved from informalisation (2016) and labour-intensive exports (2017) to labour-led growth without losing productivity (2022) and structural unemployment (2023). Inclusive growth recurs almost every year in GS3.
trend.watch: Job quality, not job numbers, is the thread across 2016–2023. Prepare structural transformation: farm to manufacturing, informality and regional disparity.

potential: "India's challenge is no longer poverty but productivity." Discuss. (15 marks)
Why has Indian manufacturing failed to absorb low-skilled labour? Suggest measures. (10 marks)

practice.q: Why has Indian manufacturing failed to absorb low-skilled labour? Suggest measures.

answer.t: Extreme poverty is down to 2.6% (World Bank), yet only 21.68% of China's and 25% of Vietnam's workers are in farming, far below India, because Indian manufacturing has not absorbed surplus labour.

pts.t: Growth in capital- and skill-intensive industries.
Compliance burden discourages scale and formal hiring.
Most enterprises stay small and low-productivity.
Raise the cost of labour-intensive exports.
Workers lack industry-ready skills.
Jobs far from the eastern belt where labour is.
Textiles, footwear, food processing, electronics assembly.
Ease compliance so firms grow and formalise.
Industrial parks in UP, Bihar and Bengal.
Apprenticeships tied to factory demand.

answer.t: Moving workers from farm to factory is the bridge from poverty reduction to mass prosperity.

title: Challenge is wages, not jobs. Expanding Jan Vishwas interventions can help
where: The Editorial Page, page 8 (Manish Sabharwal, Teamlease Services)
syllabus: GS3 › Employment; Growth and development · GS2 › Government policies; Transparency and accountability; Citizen-centric governance · GS4 › Probity in governance
summary: After decriminalising thousands of offences, the writer argues the next Jan Vishwas phase should make every rule published, knowable and trust-based, because India's problem is low wages, not a lack of jobs.
ideas: Wages, not jobs: India's problem is job quality, not quantity; a third of the workforce is in employed poverty, trapped in informal wage work and self-employment.
GS3 · Employment
India's employment challenge is low-wage informality, not joblessness; the fix lies in formal, high-wage job creation.
Regulatory cholesterol: China's per-capita GDP is five times India's (on par in 1991), not because of effort but because of India's lack of transparency, consistency and trust in law enforcement.
GS3 · Growth / GS2 · Governance
Regulatory cholesterol, not lack of talent or effort, explains much of India's per-capita income gap with China.

Six toxic thought worlds: prior approval (prohibited till permitted), enforcing the unenforceable, process as punishment, blindness to 25+ instruments below Acts, laws for edge cases, and excessive criminalisation.
GS2 · Administrative reform
India's regulatory mindset (prior approval, process as punishment, over-criminalisation) treats the citizen as a suspect.

Three next steps: Siddhant (trust-based regulation on freedom, necessity, proportionality, adopted by 30 million+ civil servants), Sangreh (a single legal record as DPI) and Ashwasan (only published obligations are enforceable).
GS2 · Citizen-centric governance
Jan Vishwas must move from decriminalisation to trust, knowability and certainty through Siddhant, Sangreh and Ashwasan.

Law must be knowable: ignorance of law is no excuse only if the State makes law accessible; earlier attempts failed on design, capacity, fragmented power, attention and technology, and lacked a binding duty to publish.
GS2 · Rule of law / Transparency
A citizen's duty to obey the law presupposes the State's duty to publish it; unpublished rules breed uncertainty and corruption.
keywords: Accumulated rules, filings and permissions that clog enterprise
Regulatory cholesterol raises the cost of formality and pushes firms into informality.
Employed poverty shows India's real problem is wage quality, not job quantity.
A prohibited-till-permitted regime presumes guilt and slows enterprise.
The procedure itself harasses the innocent
When process is punishment, even compliant citizens bear the cost of regulation.
Ignorance of the law is no excuse
Ignorantia juris holds only when the State makes the law knowable.
One machine-readable source for every legal obligation (Sangreh)
A legal DPI like Sangreh can do for compliance what UPI did for payments.
examples: Supreme Court on knowable law
Harla v State of Rajasthan (1952) rejected secret laws; B K Srinivasan (1987) moved to knowability; Viraj Impex (2019) held law operative only when published
GS2 · Judiciary / Rule of law
From Harla (1952) to Viraj Impex (2019), courts have held unpublished law cannot bind citizens.
Global single-source registers
US Federal Register, UK legislation.gov.uk, EU EUR-Lex, Singapore Statutes Online
GS2 · Comparative governance
Democracies like the US, UK and Singapore publish all binding rules in one register; India's Sangreh can follow.
Transparency of Rules Act (TORA)
Sanjeev Sanyal's draft: every enforceable obligation must be published on Sangreh
GS4
GS2 · Transparency / GS4 · Probity
TORA would make publication a precondition for enforcement, curbing discretion and corruption.
Adam Smith and the Constitution
250 years of The Wealth of Nations, 76 of the Constitution: both see government as expanding freedom
GS2 · Constitutional values / Essay
Both Adam Smith and the Constitution see the State as an enabler of freedom, not its gatekeeper.
pyqs: Trust through rule of law: Sangreh and Ashwasan are trust tools.
Job-rich, productive growth: formal high-wage jobs through deregulation.
Informalisation: regulatory cholesterol as a cause.
Civil servant as enabler: Siddhant's adoption by civil servants.

trend.t: Governance questions moved from regulatory autonomy (2015) to the e-governance interactive model (2024) and trust built through rule of law and participation (2026). Employment moved from informalisation (2016) to job-rich, productive growth (2022). GS4 (2025) asks the civil servant to be an enabler, not a regulator.
trend.watch: 'Trust' is the new keyword in GS2 and GS4. Prepare trust-based, citizen-centric governance with examples such as Jan Vishwas, GST arrest powers and self-certification.
focus: Rule of law: knowability of law

potential: "India's challenge is not jobs but wages." Examine, and suggest reforms to promote formal, high-wage employment. (15 marks)
Discuss the significance of the Jan Vishwas initiative for trust-based governance in India. What further reforms are needed? (10 marks)
"The citizen's duty to know the law presupposes the State's duty to make it knowable." Comment. (10 marks)

practice.q: Discuss the significance of the Jan Vishwas initiative for trust-based governance in India. What further reforms are needed?

answer.t: Jan Vishwas has decriminalised thousands of offences, yet a third of India's workforce remains in employed poverty, held back by regulatory cholesterol.

pts.t: The State treats citizens and firms as honest stakeholders, not suspects.
Fewer jail terms for minor lapses reduce the fear of becoming formal.
Less 'process is punishment' lets firms combine land, labour and capital.
Less discretion means fewer chances for rent-seeking.
Fewer petty cases clog courts.
It attacks the root of informality.
Freedom, necessity and proportionality to guide regulation, adopted by 30 million+ civil servants.
One machine-readable legal DPI, unifying gazettes and India Code.
Only published obligations should be enforceable.
Periodic pruning of circulars and rules.

answer.t: Jan Vishwas must move from decriminalisation to certainty, so that what is wrong with India's regulation is fixed by what is right with its democracy.

title: How welfare board will function, what changes for unorganised, gig workers
where: Economy, page 10 (Ravi Dutta Mishra & Aanchal Magazine)
syllabus: GS3 › Employment; Labour reforms · GS2 › Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections; Statutory bodies
summary: Follow-up: the Labour Ministry has notified two social security boards (40 members for unorganised workers, 22 for gig and platform workers) under the Code on Social Security.
evolution: Labour Ministry notifies the National Social Security Board under the Code on Social Security (Economy, page 23).
Details: two boards, aggregator contributions to a social security fund, and EPFO coverage widened.
ideas: Two boards, not one: a 40-member board for unorganised workers and a 22-member board for gig and platform workers, which includes aggregators such as quick-commerce and delivery platforms.
GS2 · Statutory bodies
Separate boards recognise that gig and platform workers need schemes designed for platform work.
Who pays: aggregators must contribute 1–2% of annual turnover to a social security fund, capped at 5% of what they pay workers; the fund also draws on governments, CSR and fines.
GS3 · Labour / GS2 · Welfare
Aggregator contributions put part of the cost of gig workers' security on the platforms that profit from them.
What it covers: schemes for life and disability cover, accident insurance, health and maternity benefits, old-age protection and crèches.
GS2 · Welfare
Social security for gig workers spans life-cycle risks, from maternity to old age.
Wider formal coverage: EPFO provisions now apply to all establishments with 20 or more employees, regardless of industry, not only those in the old schedule.
GS3 · Labour reforms
Extending EPFO to all establishments with 20+ workers widens formal social security.
keywords: Pooled fund for unorganised, gig and platform workers
A dedicated Social Security Fund gives gig workers' schemes a stable financing base.
Platforms paying a share of turnover towards workers' welfare
The aggregator levy shares the cost of social protection with platforms.
data: 1–2% of turnover (cap 5%)
Aggregators' contribution to the social security fund, capped at 5% of amounts payable to workers
Code on Social Security, via IE
GS3 · Labour / GS2 · Welfare
Aggregators must contribute 1–2% of turnover to gig workers' social security, capped at 5% of payouts (Code on Social Security).
examples: Aggregators on the gig workers' board
